Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-v3-train-polish-0239", "row_sha256": "c93e6b327d3901476bc4bfcf737676e0329a8dd30b62f41012bfedc86ab6afd8", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "hi mara, i'm putting together a small beginner sign language practice group at the east branch library, and could use your advice before i send the plan to the coordinator. i'm thinking of calling it a four-week ASL practice series, though i'm not sure if "series" sounds too formal for a group that is meant to feel relaxed. the library has offered us the Cedar Room on tuesday evenings in october, from 6:15 to 7:30. i haven't confirmed the dates yet because i want to check that the schedule makes sense before i ask them to hold all four evenings.

i started learning ASL last winter through a community education class, and i'm still a beginner. i can fingerspell slowly, introduce myself, and use a few everyday phrases, but i'm not able to teach grammar or answer every question about regional variation. so i don't want to present this like an instructional class or imply that people will leave fluent. i was picturing a peer practice group where we learn a small set of useful signs together, take turns rehearsing them, and write down questions to bring back to a teacher or a reliable learning resource. one person in my class said, "you learn more when you stop worrying about getting every handshape perfect," which i liked, although i also want us to be careful about practicing signs accurately.

would you look at the outline below and tell me what seems confusing or too ambitious? especially, i'm not sure how much material is reasonable in 75 minutes, and whether the order gives people enough time to practice instead of just watching me demonstrate. i have tried to make each week have one practical theme, but the list may still be too much for absolute beginners.

1. week one: names, introductions, and fingerspelling. i'd bring name cards, a printed fingerspelling chart, and a short activity where people spell their names to a partner. i'm unsure whether to include numbers in this first meeting or leave them for later, since i don't want the first night to feel like a vocabulary test.
2. week two: family and people in our lives. participants could choose a few signs from a handout and practice introducing a family member or friend. i would say clearly that people can skip personal examples and use an imaginary person instead. i don't know if the handout should include signs for different family structures or if that would make it too crowded.
3. week three: places around town and asking for directions. i thought we could use a simple printed map of the neighborhood, with the library, bus stop, clinic, and grocery store marked on it. pairs would practice asking where something is and responding, but i don't want to teach a phrase if i'm not sure the wording is natural in ASL.
4. week four: review and a short conversation practice. people could pick signs from the earlier weeks, make a small dialogue, and share it with a partner rather than in front of the whole room. i would leave the last ten minutes for questions and a list of places to keep learning. maybe there should be a better way to wrap up that doesn't turn into a performance.

i'm also trying to work out what materials are genuinely useful. right now i have access to the library's whiteboard, a laptop, and a projector, but i'd rather not spend most of the meeting with everyone looking at a screen. i could print one double-sided page for each week, with a few signs, a blank space for notes, and a link to a video from a reputable ASL learning site. do you know any resources you trust for beginners? i found several videos online, but some don't identify who made them or explain where a particular variation is used. i don't want to pass along a link just because it comes up first in a search.

there are a few practical details i haven't settled. the Cedar Room holds about twelve people around tables, and the library asked whether we expect more than eight, because they may need to arrange chairs differently. i was going to cap registration at ten, but perhaps that leaves too little room for people who decide to join at the last minute. the room has bright overhead lights and one large window; i haven't checked whether the blinds block glare from the projector. there is a step-free entrance from the parking lot, and the library says people can ask them about other access needs when they register. should i put that information in the announcement, or is there a clearer way to invite people to tell us what would help them participate?

i also wondered whether it would be useful to invite a Deaf ASL user to visit for one evening, but i don't know anyone i could ask yet, and i wouldn't want to assume someone should volunteer their time. if that is worth exploring, could you suggest a respectful way to look for a guest and ask about their fee? for now, i have not described a guest visit in the plan. i'd appreciate your thoughts on the outline, the pace, and the resource question, and whether i'm being realistic about facilitating it as a learner. if you spot a part that needs to be checked with a teacher before i use it, please point that out too. thanks for taking a look.", "output": "Hi Mara,

I'm putting together a small beginner sign language practice group at the East Branch Library, and I could use your advice before I send the plan to the coordinator. I'm thinking of calling it a four-week ASL practice series, though I'm not sure whether “series” sounds too formal for a group meant to feel relaxed. The library has offered us the Cedar Room on Tuesday evenings in October, from 6:15 to 7:30. I haven't confirmed the dates yet because I want to check that the schedule makes sense before I ask them to hold all four evenings.

I started learning ASL last winter through a community education class, and I'm still a beginner. I can fingerspell slowly, introduce myself, and use a few everyday phrases, but I'm not able to teach grammar or answer every question about regional variation. I don't want to present this as an instructional class or imply that people will leave fluent. I picture a peer practice group where we learn a small set of useful signs together, take turns rehearsing them, and write down questions to bring back to a teacher or a reliable learning resource. One person in my class said, “You learn more when you stop worrying about getting every handshape perfect,” which I liked, although I also want us to be careful about practicing signs accurately.

Would you look at the outline below and tell me what seems confusing or too ambitious? In particular, I'm not sure how much material is reasonable in 75 minutes, or whether the order gives people enough time to practice instead of just watching me demonstrate. I've tried to give each week one practical theme, but the list may still be too much for absolute beginners.

1. **Week one: Names, introductions, and fingerspelling.** I'd bring name cards, a printed fingerspelling chart, and a short activity where people spell their names to a partner. I'm unsure whether to include numbers in this first meeting or leave them for later, since I don't want the first night to feel like a vocabulary test.
2. **Week two: Family and people in our lives.** Participants could choose a few signs from a handout and practice introducing a family member or friend. I would make it clear that people can skip personal examples and use an imaginary person instead. I don't know whether the handout should include signs for different family structures or whether that would make it too crowded.
3. **Week three: Places around town and asking for directions.** I thought we could use a simple printed map of the neighborhood, with the library, bus stop, clinic, and grocery store marked on it. Pairs would practice asking where something is and responding, but I don't want to teach a phrase if I'm not sure the wording is natural in ASL.
4. **Week four: Review and a short conversation practice.** People could choose signs from the earlier weeks, create a short dialogue, and share it with a partner rather than in front of the whole group. I would leave the last ten minutes for questions and a list of places to keep learning. Maybe there's a better way to wrap up that doesn't turn into a performance.

I'm also trying to work out which materials would genuinely be useful. Right now, I have access to the library's whiteboard, a laptop, and a projector, but I'd rather not spend most of the meeting with everyone looking at a screen. I could print one double-sided page for each week, with a few signs, blank space for notes, and a link to a video from a reputable ASL learning site. Do you know any resources you trust for beginners? I found several videos online, but some don't identify who made them or explain where a particular variation is used. I don't want to pass along a link just because it comes up first in a search.

There are a few practical details I haven't settled. The Cedar Room holds about twelve people around tables, and the library asked whether we expect more than eight, because they may need to arrange the chairs differently. I was going to cap registration at ten, but perhaps that leaves too little room for people who decide to join at the last minute. The room has bright overhead lights and one large window; I haven't checked whether the blinds prevent glare from the projector. There's a step-free entrance from the parking lot, and the library says people can ask about other access needs when they register. Should I include that information in the announcement, or is there a clearer way to invite people to tell us what would help them participate?

I also wondered whether it would be useful to invite a Deaf ASL user to visit for one evening, but I don't know anyone I could ask yet, and I wouldn't want to assume someone should volunteer their time. If that is worth exploring, could you suggest a respectful way to look for a guest and ask about their fee? For now, I haven't described a guest visit in the plan. I'd appreciate your thoughts on the outline, the pace, the resource question, and whether I'm being realistic about facilitating it as a learner. If you spot anything that should be checked with a teacher before I use it, please point it out too. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "The Harbor Room fundraiser began with a simple aim: raise money for the neighborhood instrument library without making the event too complicated for a small volunteer team. The library lends guitars, keyboards, and percussion instruments to local students, and its shelves needed basic repairs as well as replacement strings, drumsticks, and power supplies. The organizers chose a Friday evening in late October, when the room was available and the library’s after-school program was not in session. They planned for about eighty guests, enough to fill the space comfortably without requiring a larger venue or additional security.

1. Set the scale before making commitments. At the first planning meeting, the volunteers listed the costs they could predict: room rental, a small public-performance fee, printing, refreshments, and a modest payment for the sound technician. They also separated those expenses from the library’s repair and supply needs. That distinction helped the group describe what donations would support without promising a specific total. “We can explain the plan clearly,” said Mina, who coordinated the library, “but we shouldn’t advertise a number until we know what the room and music will cost.” The group kept a shared spreadsheet with one tab for expected expenses and another for confirmed contributions.

2. Choose a venue and schedule that fit the program. The Harbor Room was a community space with a low stage, an accessible entrance, and chairs that volunteers could arrange in rows or around tables. A site visit helped the organizers check where performers could wait, how guests would enter, and whether the available outlets would support the keyboard and two small amplifiers. They booked the room from 4:30 to 10:00 p.m. so volunteers had time to set up before the 6:30 door opening and to clear the space afterward. The performance plan included three short sets, each separated by a brief changeover. That gave guests time to get refreshments and gave the technician time to reset microphones without rushing the musicians.

The program brought together a student guitar duo, a local singer-songwriter, and a percussion group made up of library members. The performers were asked to provide a short biography, a preferred stage arrangement, and any equipment requirements by the week before the event. The organizer did not ask them to prepare new material or promise a particular length beyond the agreed set times. In an email, Mina wrote, “If you need a stand or a direct input, tell us early; we have a limited number of each.” The technician used those replies to draft a simple stage plot and check which cables and stands the room already had.

3. Make the budget and responsibilities visible. One volunteer handled venue and performer communication, another managed the budget and donation materials, and two others coordinated refreshments and setup. No one was expected to take every task. The spreadsheet included the estimated amount, the person responsible, and a note about whether each item was confirmed. When the printer offered a discount on flyers, the treasurer recorded the revised estimate rather than treating the difference as available money. The team also agreed that cash would be counted by two volunteers together and that online donations would go through the library’s existing account. They planned to display the donation options at the entrance and beside the refreshments, with a short explanation of how the library uses contributions.

4. Keep guest information practical. The flyer named the performers, venue, door time, and suggested donation, and it stated that guests could attend even if they could not contribute. A small map showed the entrance from the main street, while the event page listed the room’s access information and a contact email for questions. The organizers avoided describing the suggested donation as a ticket price, since the room had no reserved seating and admission was not limited to paying guests. They printed a limited batch of flyers for the library, two nearby cafés, and the community center, then shared the same wording online so details would not drift between versions.

During the week of the fundraiser, the volunteers confirmed the room opening time, the technician’s arrival, the musicians’ set order, and the number of tables available. They bought refreshments only after checking the room’s rules about food and cleanup. A short checklist assigned who would bring the cash box, extension leads, tape, printed signs, and water for performers. The organizers also prepared a quiet corner near the entrance where a volunteer could answer questions without interrupting the music. They kept one spare microphone cable in the equipment box and marked the borrowed items so they could be returned to the correct people afterward.

On the evening itself, setup began with the chairs and tables, followed by the donation signs and the sound check. A volunteer at the entrance welcomed guests, pointed out the accessible route, and explained that refreshments were on a side table. Between sets, the host thanked the performers and briefly described the instrument library, without interrupting the music to make repeated donation appeals. At closing, the two cash-counting volunteers recorded the cash total together and sealed the notes in an envelope for the treasurer.
